title: New SNAP work requirements leave more than 1,000 D.C. residents without benefits - Street Sense Media

 News By Catherine Keightley November 6, 2026
 New SNAP work requirements leave more than 1,000 D.C. residents without benefits
 Food pantries have seen increasing need in recent years between rising prices and benefit cuts. Photo by Jelina Liu
 More than 1,000 D.C. residents have lost access to Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) benefits since new federal work requirements took effect in June, according to data from the D.C. Department of Human Services (DHS). 
 Another 1,000-plus residents could lose benefits in the coming month, per DHS. In July 2025, about 141,000 residents received benefits each month. That number was down to 131,000 by this July, according to federal data.
 The changes have especially impacted people experiencing homelessness, who are no longer exempt from work requirements. DHS estimates 29% of the 1,066 residents disqualified from SNAP benefits since June are experiencing housing instability. 
 The city is reviewing eligibility as recipients renew their benefits, which most do every six or 12 months, so it is likely many more people will lose access over the coming year. Of those who applied for or renewed their benefits in July, DHS identified another 1,032 residents at risk of losing benefits on Nov. 1, with an estimated 24% experiencing housing instability. The agency can’t calculate an exact number because of restrictions on information sharing between departments, a spokesperson said. 
 Decreased access to benefits comes as food insecurity in the greater Washington area has reached a five-year high. According to the Capital Area Food Bank’s 2026 Hunger Report, 38% of households in the region experienced food insecurity in the past year, as The 51st reported . The report also found 51% of surveyed SNAP recipients had to choose between paying for housing and food.

 The new work requirements, which took effect in D.C. on June 1, stem from H.R. 1 , a federal budget law passed in 2025. Under the changes, all SNAP recipients ages 18 to 64 must work, volunteer, or participate in an approved training program for at least 80 hours each month unless they qualify for an exemption .
 The law expanded work requirements to include adults ages 55 to 64 and parents and caregivers with children between 14 and 18. It also eliminated automatic exemptions for people experiencing homelessness and veterans. Now, unhoused residents must meet the requirements or qualify for another type of exemption, like for medical reasons. 
 If they don’t, they can receive just three months of benefits within three years. Because the requirements took effect this summer, that three-month period is now expiring for many Washingtonians. 
 Even for those who do still qualify, added paperwork requirements can put benefits at risk. LaMonika Jones, director of D.C. Hunger Solutions, a nonprofit initiative that works to reduce hunger and improve access to food assistance programs in the District, said the organization saw a 10% increase in calls for assistance over the summer from recipients struggling to understand the requirements and the steps they need to take to get their benefits. 
 According to Jones, recipients now have to complete an additional five-page work requirement screening form alongside their SNAP application and have an interview to determine their eligibility. For people without stable housing or consistent internet access, these requirements can make getting benefits even more difficult. 
 “We’ve seen a lot of households that are confused about all of the changes, because there’re so many that are happening so quickly,” she said. “It’s a greater burden that they’re experiencing.” 
 D.C. Hunger Solutions has helped residents navigate these changes by walking people through the steps to get medical exemptions, like getting additional paperwork and doctors’ signatures. The organization has continued offering SNAP training sessions and working with community partners to help recipients navigate the changes. The sessions are held virtually each quarter, with  recordings of past sessions available.
 DHS, meanwhile, said it is working to identify recipients who may face barriers to meeting work requirements, including people facing chronic homelessness. 
 Recipients can self-attest to experiencing chronic homelessness or facing other employment obstacles with DHS’s SNAP Work Requirement Screening form , found on the agency’s website. Filling out the form could help DHS determine whether recipients qualify for exemptions based on medical conditions, like disability, mental illness, or addiction, that would allow them to keep their benefits.
 Recipients who need help meeting the work requirements can also use DHS’s SNAP and Employment and Training (E&T) program, which connects recipients with employment and job training opportunities,  or volunteer program , which offers sessions at more than 20 sites across D.C. Beyond the work requirements, other SNAP eligibility changes have added to the uncertainty D.C. residents are facing. On Oct. 1, new federal restrictions took effect in D.C., ending SNAP eligibility for refugees and some other previously eligible noncitizens.
 Jones said D.C. Hunger Solutions has received a steady stream of questions from immigrant and mixed-status households about their eligibility and whether receiving public assistance could affect their immigration status. The organization does not yet know how many D.C. residents have lost benefits specifically because of the new noncitizen restrictions. 
 Editor’s note: Street Sense is one of 17 providers of the E&T program, and receives District funding for the program. We maintain a firewall between our journalism and services, and no one who works on the program was involved in producing this article. 
 This article originally appeared in Street Sense’s November 4, 2026 edition.
